c.tagline: Haiti's resilient capital of art, mountains, and history.

taxi.color: No official color-coding; unmarked private sedans and shared 'publique' cars, sometimes marked with a taxi sticker
taxi.fareNote: No meters are used; agree on the fare in gourdes or dollars with the driver before starting the ride.

emergency.police: 114 (Police Nationale d'Haïti) — response can be slow or unreliable given the current security crisis
emergency.medical: 118 (Croix-Rouge Haïtienne ambulance); private hospitals such as Hôpital Bernard Mevs or Hôpital Français are typically used by visitors
emergency.note: Haiti is under a U.S. State Department Level 4 'Do Not Travel' advisory due to widespread gang violence, kidnapping risk, and civil unrest; large parts of Port-au-Prince, including downtown, are considered extremely dangerous and some international flights remain suspended.

hood_landmark.Tabarre: Toussaint Louverture International Airport, Tabarre, Haiti

avoid.reason: Gang control now extends across most of the capital — Martissant, Cité Soleil, downtown and beyond — making effectively the whole city no-go for visitors.
Extreme kidnapping and armed-robbery risk city-wide, including the airport road; most governments advise do-not-travel.

hood_desc: The city's upscale commercial and social hub, full of restaurants, galleries, and long-standing hotels; the default base for business travelers and NGO staff, though caution is still required.
A quiet, gated hillside enclave just above Pétion-Ville lined with walled villas and boutique hotels, favored by diplomats and executives who prioritize privacy and security.
The long commercial corridor linking downtown to Pétion-Ville, dense with markets and workshops; suits budget-conscious travelers comfortable with heavy traffic and noise.
Home to the international airport, the U.S. Embassy, and UN offices, making it a practical if unglamorous base for arrivals, transit stops, and short business trips.
A leafy, relatively secure residential pocket popular with long-term expatriates and NGO workers seeking guesthouse-style stays close to Pétion-Ville's restaurants.

water.note: Tap water is unsafe; drink only bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or a conductor in Haitian gourdes; there is no unified fare card, app, or ticketing system. Prices follow informal route conventions or are negotiated, so carrying small bills is essential.
transit.hours: No fixed timetable; tap-taps and publiques generally run only in daylight, roughly 5am-7pm, and service thins out well before dark. There is no reliable public transport option at night.
transit.note: With no metro, tram, or formal bus network, the colorfully painted 'tap-tap' trucks and shared 'publique' taxis are the backbone of getting around; routes are learned by word of mouth rather than published maps.

ferry: Passenger ferry to La Gonâve island from the Carrefour/Montrouis area

airport.name: Toussaint Louverture International Airport (PAP)
airport.drive: 20-35 min to Pétion-Ville, longer with checkpoints or traffic

transit.m: Tap-tap/publique shared van toward Delmas or downtown (45-60 min)

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often already added at hotels and upscale restaurants; extra tipping is appreciated but not obligatory.

food.name: Griot with pikliz
food.desc: Haitis national plate: pork shoulder marinated in sour orange, braised then fried crisp, served with fiery cabbage-and-scotch-bonnet pikliz.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: Long-established Haitian kitchen whose griot and lambi are its signature dishes.

places.name: Quartier Latin
places.note: Veteran restaurant and jazz room serving Creole classics in the evening.

places.name: Kinam Hotel
places.note: Gingerbread-style hotel with a courtyard restaurant; conditions change fast, check ahead.

food.name: Soup joumou
food.desc: Squash soup with beef, pasta and root vegetables, eaten every 1 January to mark independence; once forbidden to the enslaved, now a symbol.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: Reliable place to find the soup, especially around the new year.

places.name: Kinam Hotel
places.note: Hotel dining room that keeps traditional Haitian dishes on the menu.

places.name: L'Observatoire de Boutillier
places.note: Creole cooking with a panoramic view over the bay; verify opening before going up.

food.name: Tassot
food.desc: Goat or beef marinated in citrus, epis herb paste and chilli, dried then deep-fried until chewy-crisp; eaten with fried plantain and pikliz.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: Full spread of Haitian fried meats with a warm room and live music some nights.

places.name: Quartier Latin
places.note: Creole plates alongside a bar and music programme.

places.name: Presse Cafe
places.note: Casual all-day spot popular with locals for Haitian standards.

food.name: Diri djon djon
food.desc: Rice cooked in the inky liquor of dried Haitian black mushrooms, turning it grey-black and deeply savoury; usually served with shrimp or meat.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: One of the safest bets in the city for the classic mushroom rice.

places.name: L'Observatoire de Boutillier
places.note: Creole and international menu on the ridge above the capital.

places.name: Kinam Hotel
places.note: Hotel kitchens are often the most consistently open option in unstable periods.

food.name: Akra and fritay
food.desc: Fritay is the fried snack platter: akra malanga fritters, marinad dough fritters, banann peze plantain and pikliz, sold from streetside pans.

places.name: Place St-Pierre
places.note: Fritay vendors set up around the square in the late afternoon.

places.name: Presse Cafe
places.note: Sit-down version of the fritay platter if street stands feel unwise.

places.name: Muncheez
places.note: Home-grown Haitian chain, dependable and popular with young Port-au-Prince.

food.name: Lambi
food.desc: Conch simmered in a Creole sauce of tomato, pepper and epis, or grilled; the seafood dish Haitians order first on the coast.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: Lambi is named alongside griot as the house speciality.

places.name: Quartier Latin
places.note: Seafood Creole dishes served late with music.

places.name: L'Observatoire de Boutillier
places.note: Worth the climb for the view; call ahead, access depends on the security situation.

food.name: Rhum Barbancourt
food.desc: Haitian rum distilled from fresh sugarcane juice since 1862 and aged in oak; sipped neat, or in a rum sour with lime. Prestige is the local beer.

places.name: Quartier Latin
places.note: Bar and live-music room; the obvious place for an aged Barbancourt.

places.name: Kinam Hotel
places.note: Courtyard bar under the trees, a long-standing expatriate meeting point.

places.name: Presse Cafe
places.note: Relaxed cafe-bar for rum drinks and cold Prestige.

food.name: Kremas
food.desc: Thick, sweet cream liqueur of rum, coconut milk, condensed milk, lime zest, cinnamon and star anise; poured at Christmas and every celebration.

places.name: Papaye Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Haitian menu that usually finishes with a glass of kremas.

places.name: Place St-Pierre
places.note: Market and street vendors sell homemade kremas in recycled bottles.

places.name: Muncheez
places.note: Local chain where kremas turns up in shakes and desserts.

landmarks: Citadelle Laferrière
A colossal mountaintop fortress built after Haiti's independence, ranked among the largest fortresses in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Sans-Souci Palace
The dramatic ruins of King Henri Christophe's opulent royal palace, often called the 'Caribbean Versailles,' evoking Haiti's revolutionary-era grandeur.
Cathédrale Notre-Dame de l'Assomption
The storied pink-and-white cathedral of Port-au-Prince, an emblem of the capital's skyline despite the devastating damage it suffered in 2010.
Marché en Fer (Iron Market)
A striking wrought-iron market hall with distinctive red towers, bustling with vendors selling crafts, art, and goods in the heart of downtown.
Le Marron Inconnu (Unknown Maroon)
A powerful bronze statue of a triumphant, chain-breaking freedom fighter blowing a conch shell, symbolizing Haiti's hard-won independence from slavery.
Musée du Panthéon National Haïtien (MUPANAH)
An underground museum showcasing Haiti's revolutionary history, including Toussaint Louverture's relics and the anchor from Columbus's ship Santa María.
Bassin Bleu
A series of stunning turquoise waterfall pools tucked into a canyon near Jacmel, reached by a scenic hike and popular for swimming and photos.
National Palace (Palais National)
Haiti's historic white presidential palace, a symbol of the nation's political life whose iconic domes have long anchored the Port-au-Prince skyline.
Champ de Mars
The capital's grand central plaza and public park, ringed by statues of revolutionary heroes and government buildings, and a hub of city life.
Hôtel Oloffson
A gabled Victorian gingerbread mansion turned hotel in the Pacot district, long a gathering place for writers and musicians and the model for Graham Greene's novel The Comedians.

train.note: Haiti has no passenger railway. Overland travel is by bus or car only.

bus.note: Capital Coach Line still advertises daily coaches between Port-au-Prince and Santo Domingo, but reliability is very uncertain: gang violence controls much of Port-au-Prince, the Dominican Republic-Haiti land border has faced repeated closures, and Caribe Tours suspended its Haiti service years ago over insecurity. Haiti is a Level 4 'Do Not Travel' destination - confirm the route is actually running and check government travel advisories before booking.

ferry.note: There are no scheduled international passenger ferries from Port-au-Prince. Given the ongoing security crisis, no reliable domestic passenger boat service can be recommended either.
